Next 7 Days (through Friday)

Very appropriate Halloween weather is in store over the next 24 
hours. Low stratus that lingered through the entirety of the day 
Friday is transitioning into widespread fog tonight, including an
expansion in area. The plains will likely see the most widespread
dense fog this morning with visibility of 1/4 mile or less 
possible. This is all being aided by weak upslope (easterly) 
winds across the CWA. Due to this, the other area that could see 
dense fog will be in the foothills of the east facing aspects of 
the mountains. 

Also occuring this morning are some scattered showers, especially
over the western 2/3 of the CWA. Ahead of the main upper level 
low, a lobe of energy is pivoting through eastern ID into Central 
Montana. This is bringing us scattered rain and snow showers this
morning. As the vort max continues to move through the area 
quickly, the coverage in showers is forecast to decrease through 
the afternoon and evening hours. That being said, there is still 
a 20-40% chance of precip for much of the CWA through the evening 
hours. So it might be a good idea to carry an umbrella this 
evening in case you need keep that costume dry. 

Due to the fact that there will be minimal change in the overall
weather regime through the day today, another round of fog is
forecast tonight as well. All of the same conditions remain in
place, however as the parent system moves in Sunday morning, this
will help clear out some of the fog west of Billings as rain
showers begin. In the same way we saw last evening, the fog could
develop right after sunset so be prepared for a potentially foggy
Halloween Night!

The upper level low that is currently situated just off of the 
coast of the PNW will slowly move due east into the Northern 
Rockies through the day today and Sunday. By Sunday AM, much of 
south-central MT will be seeing some form of precip. Note that 
snow levels will start out high before falling overnight Sunday 
into Monday morning as we start to see more cold air advect in. 
Even the NBM 25th percentile keeps the snow at or above 8kft 
through the day Sunday before gradually dropping down to 5kft 
Monday. This is the low end solution so levels will likely be a 
touch higher than this. Precipitation will end from west to east 
during the day Monday. 

In terms of precip totals there is actually some good news. The
current forecast is that as surface cyclogenesis occurs to our
south, the wrap-around precip band will set up over our eastern 
CWA. This region has missed out on much of the rainfall events 
over the past several months and is therefore in an extreme 
drought (D3). The current forecast is for this region to see 
widespread totals of around 0.5" with locally higher amounts. The 
NBM 75th percentile even has some locations seeing up to 1.5" of 
rainfall for the entire event.

Although snow will not be a big part of this event, it will likely
be the first impactful snow of the year for the Bighorn Mountains.
The current 10-90 percentile spread for Burgess Junction is 2-14"
with the mean sitting around 7". This will impact any recreation 
in the high country. One of the largest forecast questions 
surrounding the Bighorns is the forecast wind direction on 
Monday. This system will have PWAT values around 200% of normal so
there will be ample moisture wrapping around the cyclone, however
a few degrees change in the wind direction could make a huge 
difference regarding just how much upslope the eastern side of the
terrain sees. As of right now, most models are showing nearly a 
perfect north direction in the wind to start the day Monday before
slowly becoming NW. This will be something we have to keep a 
close eye on as more high-res models solutions come in. Speaking 
of the wind for this area, it may just be the most impactful part 
of this system.

As the surface low develops and quickly deepens Monday, winds will
pick up as a result. By Monday afternoon, the ECMWF ensemble shows
a 997mb low over the Great Plains, while the GFS ensemble shows it
as low as 995mb. With a tight gradient between the low and the
developing 1024 high associated with the CAA, a good gradient 
will set up over eastern MT/WY. This flow will be locally enhanced
near Sheridan as it funnels around the Bighorn Mountains. Gusts 
in the 40s mph Monday afternoon in Sheridan are almost certain at
this point, however there is a greater than 50% chance that we 
see gusts in the mid 50s mph range Monday afternoon/evening as 
well. These wind speeds are also forecast in the Bighorns during 
this timeframe as well. This could result in sharply reduced 
visibility due to the winds in combination with falling snow. 

Although details are still quite fuzzy past this early week event,
the overall pattern seems to be decently clear. It looks like we
